Neonates of the Brazilian snake-necked turtle (Hydromedusa maximiliani) emerge possessing a modest plastron length of 2.85 centimeters [Lb = 2.85 centimeters], a dimension that reflects the limited space available within its leathery-shelled eggs. Field surveys consistently report hatchlings with a wet weight of 7.8 grams [Wwb = 7.8 grams], placing this species among the smaller-bodied pleurodires at the onset of exogenous feeding. Incubation experiments conducted under controlled thermal conditions show that the age at birth is approximately 275 days [ab = approximately 275 days] when eggs are maintained at a steady 24 °C [T = 24 °C]; this prolonged developmental period, spanning nearly nine months, is typical of chelids that inhabit cool, montane streams in southeastern Brazil. During this phase of progressive yolk utilization, the embryo relies entirely on endogenous reserves until the moment of egg caruncle action initiates shell pipping. The relatively small hatchling size likely imposes strong selective pressures during the juvenile stage, as young individuals must quickly locate suitable foraging microhabitats to sustain their early growth trajectory.

Males of Hydromedusa maximiliani follow a notably longer developmental schedule to reach reproductive activation compared to females. Under the same standard thermal regime of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], which is characteristic of their natural stream habitats, the time from birth to the onset of puberty spans approximately 17 years [tp = approximately 17 years], a value derived from long-term mark-recapture studies of known-age individuals. During this extended pre-reproductive juvenile phase, males attain a plastron length of about 10.2 centimeters [Lp = about 10.2 centimeters] before initiating gametogenesis. In contrast, females invest energy more rapidly into somatic growth and reach gonadal maturation sooner, achieving a plastron length of roughly 8.8 centimeters [Lp = roughly 8.8 centimeters] at puberty, which occurs roughly 9 years [tp = roughly 9 years] after the hatching e at a temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]vent. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in maturation timing is consistent with patterns observed across other long-lived freshwater turtles, where earlier female maturity is often linked to the energetic advantages of attaining a larger body size before reproductive effort begins.

As individuals transition into the reproductively active adult stage, the ultimate size achieved differs substantially between the sexes. Females eventually attain a maximum plastron length of 11.8 centimeters [Li = 11.8 centimeters] and an ultimate wet weight of 520 grams [Wwi = 520 grams], representing a considerable increase from their neonatal mass. Males, however, reach a slightly larger ultimate plastron length of 12.6 centimeters [Li = 12.6 centimeters] despite having a later onset of puberty, a pattern that is somewhat unusual among chelonians and warrants further investigation into the biomechanical or ecological drivers of this dimorphism. The larger body size of males may confer advantages during intrasexual combat or territory defense within the rocky stream channels they inhabit. Adult body condition in this species is highly dependent on the availability of aquatic invertebrate prey, with gravid females in particular needing to accumulate substantial lipid stores to support yolk deposition during each reproductive cycle. The asymptotic mass appears to be reached only after several decades of sustained growth.

The maximum longevity documented for Hydromedusa maximiliani under seminatural captive conditions, at a constant 24 °C [T = 24 °C], extends to 100 years [am = 100 years], placing this chelid among the longest-lived freshwater turtles in South America. This remarkable lifespan is accompanied by a notably low daily reproductive output; although females produce only a single clutch of 1 to 3 parchment-shelled eggs per breeding event [N_R_i = 1 to 3 parchment-shelled eggs per breeding event], and typically generate just one such clutch annually [F_R_i = one such clutch annually], the cumulative reproductive career spanning many decades allows for substantial lifetime fecundity. The maximum reproduction rate, observed in prime-aged females under optimal thermal conditions at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], equates to approximately 3 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 3 eggs per year]. This low annual output is characteristic of a slow life-history strategy, where the species invests heavily in the survival of each individual offspring rather than producing large numbers of eggs.

Comparative analyses within the family Chelidae reveal that Hydromedusa maximiliani exhibits one of the slowest life-history paces among its congeners, likely an adaptation to the nutrient-poor, cool-water environments it occupies. The prolonged embryonic development, with ab hatchlings emerging after 275 days [ab = 275 days] at 24 °C [T = 24 °C], contrasts sharply with the faster incubation times of tropical chelids exposed to warmer thermal regimes. This slow pace extends into the adult phase, where the maximum wet weight of 520 grams [Wwi = 520 grams] in females is modest relative to body masses exceeding one kilogram in related species such as Hydromedusa tectifera. The combination of a century-long lifespan, delayed puberty in both sexes, and extremely low annual reproductive output underscores a bet-hedging strategy finely tuned to stable but low-productivity aquatic habitats.
